name: bantamkit-mcp

tools.name: memory_save
tools.description: Save ONE durable fact to persistent memory — a preference the user stated, a decision, the fix that worked — so a future session can recall it. Use it only for facts a future session needs; never for anything derivable from the repo, git history or docs, nor for one-off state of this conversation. To find a fact use memory_recall; to change one, save again under its EXACT name, which replaces it in place; to free room call memory_compact. Refused with nothing written, each with its own sentence: a description too close to an existing fact's (the reply names that fact — save under that SAME name or skip, never rename to force a copy), a spelling that normalises onto an existing name (`Deploy Command` onto `deploy-command`), and a save that would push the always-loaded index over its byte budget (the reply names the remedy). Every save lands in the writable project store (.bantamkit/memory), never in the profile or a read-only grant, and is appended to the usage ledger. Optional outcome (error|success) tags a lesson and status: done closes a project fact; nothing here archives — that is the operator's bantamkit-memory candidates/merge.

type.description: What kind of fact: `user` (who the user is, their role and preferences), `feedback` (a correction or confirmed way of working, with the why), `project` (ongoing work, a decision, a constraint), `reference` (a URL, ticket or dashboard pointer).

description.description: One line written to match the FUTURE recall query, not to summarize the body

keywords.description: Words the user will type when they need this fact, in the user's own language as well as English (e.g. Thai and English terms)

queries.description: The prompts a user would type when this fact is what they need: three in the user's language and three in English, at most 8, each at most 200 characters

outcome.description: What the lesson records: `error` (a failure to avoid) or `success` (a way that worked). Only on feedback and project facts; refused on user and reference. Read back by `bantamkit-memory list --outcome` and by memory_recall's `outcome` filter.

status.description: Lifecycle of a project fact. Save an existing name with `done` when the work it describes has shipped; `bantamkit-memory candidates` lists done facts for the operator to archive. Absent means active; `active` is never written.

tools.name: memory_recall
tools.description: Search persistent memory for facts a past session saved. Call it BEFORE starting a task that resembles past work, and when the user refers to something decided earlier; use memory_save to add a fact, and memory_compact or memory_dream only to tidy the store — this tool never changes what a fact says. Reads every layer in order — the project store, any read-only grants in .bantamkit/config.yaml, then the machine-wide profile — and returns the top word matches, never fewer than the store default of 3 when that many match; a query that is exactly a fact's name returns that fact alone. Pass `file` instead of `query` to see the facts linked to a file. Why it is not read-only: every hit is appended to the usage ledger (~/.bantamkit/usage/<store-id>.jsonl) as a recall event — the staleness order memory_compact archives by — and a project fact file still in the 0.35.x format is rewritten once into the current one; both are best-effort and never fail a recall. A fact file that cannot be read is named in the reply, never silently skipped. Pass outcome: error to see only recorded failures.

query.description: Words a past-you would have used to describe the fact

k.description: Facts wanted, clamped to 1..5. Raised to the store default of 3 when smaller; never lowered below it.

include_archived.description: Also search facts compaction moved to archive/. Archived matches come after the live ones, tagged [archived].

file.description: A tracked file, or the shortest unique suffix of one (store.ts, memory/store.ts). Returns the facts linked to it and when it was last touched; query is then ignored.

outcome.description: Keep only facts saved with this outcome — `error` answers "what failed before", `success` "what worked". Facts with no outcome are dropped from the answer; omit it for the normal search.

tools.name: validate_json
tools.description: Validate candidate output text against a JSON Schema and say what is wrong. Answers {valid, feedback}: when invalid, hand `feedback` back to the model and retry — it says where the document fails and quotes the offending value, clipped to 200 characters; when valid, `feedback` is null. Use it on any JSON a model produced before acting on it; for a shift-work checkpoint call shiftwork_status or shiftwork_clock_in instead, which validate against the shipped checkpoint schema themselves. `output` may be a bare JSON value; otherwise the first fenced code block, else the first object or array in the text, is what gets validated. `$schema` selects draft-04, draft-06, draft-07, 2019-09 or 2020-12 (the default). `$ref` resolves only inside the one schema given (`#`, `#/...`, `#name`): a remote reference or an embedded `$id` is refused with its own sentence, never fetched. `pattern` is Python re syntax without inline flags, look-behind, backreferences, atomic, possessive or conditional groups or \N{...}, and all of a document's patterns share 500 ms: past that the answer is one refusal sentence naming the pattern that ran out, not a partial validation. Reads nothing but its two arguments and writes nothing.

output.title: Output
output.description: The text to validate, as the model returned it: a JSON value, or prose holding a fenced code block or a JSON object/array.

schema.title: Schema
schema.description: The JSON Schema object (draft-04 through 2020-12) the output must satisfy; `$ref` may only point inside it.

tools.name: shiftwork_clock_in
tools.description: Shift-work clock-in: validate the checkpoint against the checkpoint schema and return the brief of ONE unit — {unit, role, invariants, handoff, do_not, files} — to hand to the agent you spawn, verbatim. Call it once per unit, right before spawning; use shiftwork_plan first to see the `ready` batch when several units are to run at once, and shiftwork_clock_out, not this tool, when a unit finishes. The unit briefed is plan.cursor, or `unit_id` when given; either way it must be in shiftwork_plan's `ready` — a done or dropped cursor, a cursor whose dependencies have not run, or a `unit_id` naming no unit answers {"result": "error", "reason": "unit <id> is not ready; ready is <a, b>"}, and the batch view's own refusals (cycle, unknown dependency, unreadable checkpoint) pass through verbatim. The other outcomes, never exceptions: `escalate` when handoff.open_questions is non-empty (stop and ask the user) or when the cursor names no unit, `success` when every unit is done or dropped, `error` when the checkpoint fails validation. It never moves plan.cursor; clock_out does. What it WRITES: on result=brief, and only then, one line {event: brief, ts, unit, role} appended to <checkpoint>.log.jsonl — best-effort, so a log it cannot write costs the brief nothing. That line is what later lets clock_out accept the unit while the cursor is elsewhere and sets `briefed` on its accounting line. The checkpoint file itself is never modified. See docs/shiftwork.md.

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint
checkpoint.description: Path to the shift-work checkpoint JSON file (by convention .shiftwork/checkpoint.json in the repo the job works on), absolute or relative to the server's working directory. The same file shiftwork_plan, shiftwork_clock_in and shiftwork_clock_out take; it must validate against assets/schemas/shiftwork-checkpoint.json.

unit_id.title: Unit Id
unit_id.description: The unit to brief instead of plan.cursor; it must be in shiftwork_plan's `ready` for this checkpoint. Omit it, or pass null, to brief the cursor unit.

tools.name: shiftwork_clock_out
tools.description: Shift-work clock-out: record that a unit finished — set its status, advance plan.cursor, merge `handoff_patch` into handoff, push `history_entry` onto the 5-entry history ring, and append one accounting line to <checkpoint>.log.jsonl. Call it once per unit after its agent returns: shiftwork_clock_in briefs, this tool closes, and shiftwork_status reads what both wrote. The whole mutated document is validated against the checkpoint schema BEFORE one atomic write, so a failure writes nothing and answers {"result": "error", "reason": ...}; nothing is ever deleted from the checkpoint. `unit_id` must be plan.cursor — which needs no brief and clocks out with briefed=false — or a unit clock_in briefed since its own last clock-out; any other id is refused with `unit X is not the cursor unit Y`. `handoff_patch` and `history_entry` are both required arguments: pass `{}` to leave handoff unchanged, and give history_entry at least `unit` and `outcome`. plan.cursor then moves to the head of the ready batch recomputed on the new document — plan.units order over the remaining non-terminal units when the graph cannot batch, `unit_id` when none remain. The accounting line carries unit, role, status, ts and `briefed` (written by the runtime, never taken from you: true only when a brief was issued since this unit's LAST clock-out) plus your `accounting` fields when given. When job.roles names this unit's role, `accounting.model` must be on that role's list, spelled exactly, or nothing is written — see the `model` property.

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint
checkpoint.description: Path to the shift-work checkpoint JSON file (by convention .shiftwork/checkpoint.json in the repo the job works on), absolute or relative to the server's working directory. The same file shiftwork_plan, shiftwork_clock_in and shiftwork_clock_out take; it must validate against assets/schemas/shiftwork-checkpoint.json.

unit_id.title: Unit Id
unit_id.description: The unit being clocked out. Must be plan.cursor, or a unit briefed since its own last clock-out: clock_in briefs the cursor unit by default and, when its unit_id names one, any unit shiftwork_plan reports in `ready` — and that brief is what lets clock_out accept a unit the cursor is not on.

status.title: Status
status.description: The unit's new status; the same five values the checkpoint schema allows on plan.units[].status.

handoff_patch.title: Handoff Patch
handoff_patch.description: Shallow-merged into `handoff`: only these four keys exist there, and a key outside them is refused by the schema check. Required; `{}` leaves `handoff` unchanged.

open_questions.description: The autonomy switch: empty = driver keeps cycling, non-empty = STOP and ask.

do_not.description: Negative space — near-mistakes past sessions made.

notes.description: Free-form prose for the next session, one string; the empty string clears it.

history_entry.title: History Entry
history_entry.description: Pushed onto the 5-entry `history` ring; `unit` and `outcome` are required, `notes` optional, other keys pass through.

unit.description: The unit this entry is about — normally the `unit_id` being clocked out.

outcome.description: What happened, in a few words: done, blocked on X, dropped because Y.

notes.description: Optional free text for the next session reading the ring.

anyOf.description: Per-unit cost. Written verbatim, beside ts/unit/role/status, as one line of <checkpoint>.log.jsonl - the ledger the N-sessions experiment reads. The keys named here have fixed meanings so a reader holding only the ledger knows what each number counts, in which unit, and which model produced it; any other key passes through unchanged, except the five the runtime writes itself — unit, role, status, ts, event — which are refused (result=error) before anything is written; a self-reported briefed is overwritten, not refused. Lines written before this schema existed may spell these differently; the schema governs new writes only.

tokens.description: Tokens the unit consumed as the harness's subagent counter reports them: every class it reports (input, output, cache creation) summed, EXCLUDING cache reads. In a non-null accounting line it is required — a line without it is refused before anything is written; only `accounting: null`, the default, is exempt, and that logs no cost at all. A rounded self-estimate is allowed only if `note` says it is one; a unit whose cost is unknown cannot be compared with any other.

cache_read_tokens.description: Tokens the unit's requests served from prompt cache, kept OUT of `tokens` because they dominate a real session's traffic and would swamp the work signal. Optional: omit it when the harness reports no such figure - a written 0 means the unit read nothing from cache.

duration_ms.description: Wall-clock from spawning the subagent to its final message, in whole milliseconds. In a non-null line it is required, and it is the only duration key with a defined meaning: older lines carry `duration`, `duration_min` or `duration_s`, which this schema neither reads nor renames.

model.description: The exact identifier of the model the subagent actually ran on (e.g. `claude-sonnet-5`) and nothing else - a caveat about how it was chosen belongs in `note`. Not required here: when the checkpoint's job.roles names this unit's role, clock_out already requires it and refuses a value off that role's list, spelled exactly; a checkpoint with no job.roles leaves it optional. This schema does not change that gate.

tool_uses.description: Tool calls the subagent made, as the harness counts them. Optional; it is the denominator that makes `tokens` comparable across units of different size (per-unit cost is linear in tool calls, not in unit length).

note.description: Free text for what the fields above cannot say: that `tokens` is an estimate, that this is a retry or a second scope under the same unit id, what a harness counter excludes. Anything that is not a model identifier goes here, not in `model`.

accounting.title: Accounting
accounting.description: Per-unit cost line, or null (the default) to log a line with no cost figures at all. A non-null line must carry `tokens` and `duration_ms`; `model` is required when job.roles names this unit's role. The object shape is described below.

tools.name: shiftwork_status
tools.description: Shift-work status: where ONE checkpoint file stands — units counted by status, the unit plan.cursor points at, how many handoff.open_questions are waiting, and the last history entry. Call it first when resuming a job or answering 'where is job X'; it is the cheap read before any clock-in. It does not say WHICH units may run now — that is shiftwork_plan, the dependency batches — and it says nothing about the server itself, which is bantamkit_status. Every fact is read from the checkpoint on this call, nothing is cached, and a checkpoint that is missing, not valid JSON or failing the checkpoint schema answers {"result": "error", "reason": "<sentence>"} instead of a partial summary — the same refusals shiftwork_plan and shiftwork_clock_in give for that file. With `search`, it also returns the lines of jobs Retention archived under the checkpoint's .shiftwork/archive/ that hold every word of the query. Opens only the checkpoint (and that archive directory when `search` is given); writes nothing, not even the log shiftwork_clock_in appends to.

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint
checkpoint.description: Path to the shift-work checkpoint JSON file (by convention .shiftwork/checkpoint.json in the repo the job works on), absolute or relative to the server's working directory. The same file shiftwork_plan, shiftwork_clock_in and shiftwork_clock_out take; it must validate against assets/schemas/shiftwork-checkpoint.json.

search.description: Also search jobs Retention archived under this checkpoint's .shiftwork/archive/: every line holding all the query's words, as {job, file, line}.

tools.name: build_identity
tools.description: Which bantamkit build is answering you, readable mid-call. Returns `build_id` — a content fingerprint of the running source and the asset pack it loads — plus the paths it was computed over. Call it when one MCP server name may resolve to more than one install: two endpoints reporting the same `version` are the SAME build only if their `build_id` matches, because a version string moves on release bumps and not on builds. Any fact that cannot be derived comes back as {"unavailable": "<reason>"} and is named in the `unavailable` list — never omitted, never a placeholder that reads as a value. Takes no arguments and reads no state. Use bantamkit_status when the question is whether the server is healthy or which store it is bound to — that report includes this fingerprint; call this tool when you need only the fingerprint, as JSON, to compare two endpoints.

tools.name: bantamkit_status
tools.description: Is bantamkit working, and which bantamkit? Returns a short report a person can read in the transcript: `bantamkit Active 🟢` or `bantamkit Degraded 🟠` on the first line, then the version and `build_id` of the code answering, the surfaces it serves, the memory store it is bound to with its index size against its budget, whether the event log is on, and — when degraded — every condition in full with what to do about it. Call it when the user asks whether the server is alive or working, when a bantamkit tool answered oddly and you need to know whether the server is the reason, or when a reply arrived carrying a `bantamkit degraded` footer and you want the rest of it. Every fact is observed at call time from the server's own state; nothing is a heartbeat or a cached verdict. Takes no arguments, writes nothing, and never echoes another call's arguments. build_identity answers only the `build_id` fingerprint, as JSON, when all you need is to compare two installs; shiftwork_status reports a job, not the server.

tools.name: memory_compact
tools.description: Free room in persistent memory when `memory_save` was refused for budget. Archives the stalest facts of the writable project store until a fact as large as the biggest one kept will fit, and returns what moved — every archived name with its type and description. Nothing is deleted: archived facts leave the index but stay on disk under archive/, memory_recall with `include_archived` still finds them, and bringing one back is an operator action rather than a tool — `bantamkit-memory restore <name>` (Node) or `python -m bantamkit.memory restore <name>` (Python) on the store; no tool deletes a fact. Read-only grants and the profile layer are never touched. Call it after a budget refusal, then retry the save; calling it under budget archives nothing and says so. It is not the pass for two copies of one name across layers — that is memory_dream.

reserve.description: Bytes of index headroom to free below the budget: the target is `budget - reserve`, a negative value counts as 0, any value is capped at half the budget, and 0 compacts to the budget itself. Omit for the default: the room the degraded-index warning demands (the budget minus `(90 * budget - 1) // 100`) plus the size of the largest index line the store holds -- at the default 24000-byte budget with a 39-byte largest line that is 2401 + 39 = 2440, a 21560-byte target.

tools.name: skill_audit
tools.description: Price the skill catalogue every session pays for, and name the collisions in it. A skill's `description:` frontmatter is loaded into the agent's context in EVERY session; its body is read only when the skill is invoked, so the descriptions are the standing bill. Call it before adding or retiring a skill, or when two skills keep firing on the same phrase. Walks `root` for `<marketplace>/<plugin>/<version>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and answers one JSON document: `roots`, `skills` (counted), `catalogue_bytes` (UTF-8 bytes of their `description:` values), `findings` and `omissions`. A degraded server adds the footer as its last key, `bantamkit_degraded`. Read `findings` first — each is `{kind, severity, skills, detail}`: `shared-trigger-phrase` (high; two skills quote the same literal phrase, so which fires is a coin flip), `catalogue-over-budget` (high; only when `budget` is given), `never-invoked` (low; only when `usage` is given), `frontmatter-malformed` and `name-mismatch` (medium). Then `omissions`: counted skills plus omissions account for every SKILL.md found, each `{subject, count, size, what}` with subject one of `plugin-not-enabled`, `duplicate-skill`, `stale-version`, `unreadable-file`, `unparsed-frontmatter`. The tool reads nothing but `root`; the three facts a directory cannot answer come from the caller — `enabled` (plugin ids the host has switched on, `<plugin>@<marketplace>`; the cache also holds disabled plugins, so without it the bill is inflated), `usage` (call counts per skill) and `versions` (the version directory the host serves per plugin; a plugin absent from it gets the directory name that sorts LAST in byte order, which is wrong for `10.0.0` against `9.0.0`). Refused with their own sentence, never as a partial answer: an unknown `check`, a negative `budget`, an EMPTY `root`, a `root` that is missing or is a file. Full rules in docs/skill-audit.md.

root.description: Directory to scan for SKILL.md files, absolute or relative to the server's working directory. It must name a directory: the empty string is refused rather than resolved, because resolving it would audit whatever directory the server happens to be standing in

enabled.description: Plugin ids that are switched on, `<plugin>@<marketplace>`; when given only skills under those plugins are counted, when omitted every skill under `root` counts

usage.description: Skill id (`<plugin>:<name>`) to call count, the caller's own measurement; a counted skill absent from a supplied map is treated as zero

check.description: Which family of findings to report; default `all`. `skills`, `catalogue_bytes` and `omissions` are reported whatever this says

budget.description: Catalogue byte budget; `catalogue-over-budget` is only reported when this is given

versions.description: Plugin id (`<plugin>@<marketplace>`) to the version directory name the host actually serves; when a plugin is named here that directory is resolved whatever byte order would have said, and a plugin absent from it falls back to byte order

tools.name: memory_dream
tools.description: Consolidate the memories the project layer and the machine-wide profile layer hold under the SAME NAME, and say exactly what changed. Byte-identical copies collapse to one; a pair that has diverged is UNIONED — every claim from both copies survives, never a winner-takes-all — and a relative date in a body is annotated with the day it resolves to against that fact's own mtime, never against today. The survivor stays in the writable project layer and the profile copy MOVES to that store's archive/: nothing is deleted, and bringing a consumed copy back is an operator action, not a tool — `bantamkit-memory restore <name>` or `python -m bantamkit.memory restore <name>` on the profile store. This is a correctness pass, not a token saving: the profile index is derived at read time and is not loaded from a prompt, so consolidating it frees approximately no bytes — what it buys is one copy of a ruling instead of two that can disagree. It defaults to a DRY RUN because the profile store is machine-wide: a memory archived out of it stops answering for every other project on this machine that has no store of its own. Read the plan first, then call it again with dry_run false to apply it. For room in the index call memory_compact instead; for the facts themselves, memory_recall.

dry_run.description: Preview only. True (the default) performs every read, merge and projection and writes nothing. Pass false to apply the plan.

tools.name: token_ledger
tools.description: What a session actually cost, read off the host's own transcripts. Walks `root` for `*.jsonl` transcripts — the host writes `<cwd-slug>/<session>.jsonl` and `<cwd-slug>/<session>/subagents/*.jsonl` beneath `~/.claude/projects` — and answers ONE JSON document: `root`, `transcripts`, `lines`, `requests` (distinct API requests), `totals` (the four classes: `input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `output_tokens`), `sessions` (one row each), `omissions`, and `cost` only when `model` is given. A degraded server adds the footer as its last key, `bantamkit_degraded`. Call it to answer 'what did this work cost' from the API's own `usage` blocks; nothing is estimated. Point `root` at ONE project's slug directory: there is no time window or summary mode, so a whole-corpus call answers a row per session ever recorded and blows the host's tool-result cap. The four classes are priced separately: on a real prompt 98.1 % of the tokens were `cache_read`. Counting is per `requestId`, never per line: one response is written as several records with the same `usage`, so the dedupe spans the whole walk and every later copy is a `duplicate-request` omission. A subagent's transcript carries its PARENT's `sessionId`, so its cost lands in the parent row as `sidechain_requests`. `lines` equals `requests` plus the sum of every omission's `count`, always. An omission is `{subject, count, what}`; `what` names the first site as `<relpath>:<line>` plus `and N more`. `cost` needs a rate: the shipped price table has none, so `{"unavailable": "no rate recorded for model ..."}` is the NORMAL answer, not an error; a rate enters through `$BANTAMKIT_PRICES` or `prices`. Refused with their own sentence: an EMPTY `root`, a `root` that is missing or is a file, an EMPTY `model`, and a token total above 2**53-1. The record rule and the nine omission subjects: docs/ledger.md.

root.description: Directory of host transcripts to walk, absolute or relative to the server's working directory; `~/.claude/projects` is where the host keeps them on this machine. It must name a directory: the empty string is refused rather than resolved, because resolving it would read whatever directory the server happens to be standing in

model.description: Model to price the totals as, e.g. the id an assistant record's `message.model` carries. Omit it and no `cost` key is reported at all; name one with no recorded rate and `cost` is `{"unavailable": ...}`, which is what the shipped table answers for every model

prices.description: Price table to read instead of `$BANTAMKIT_PRICES` or the shipped one; only consulted when `model` is given. A malformed table is a configuration fault and stops with its own sentence, rather than being reported as an unpriced model

tools.name: work_plan
tools.description: Work plan: turn a dependency graph you hand it into the batches that may run in parallel — pure computation over `nodes`: no file opened, no path taken, nothing mutated. Use it when the graph is in your hands (tasks with depends_on); use shiftwork_plan when the graph is a shift-work checkpoint on disk, which it reads for you under the same batching rules. Batch k holds every node whose dependencies all sit in batches below k; `sequence` is the batches flattened; `width` is the largest batch — the fan-out an orchestrator must afford. Inside a batch: priority descending, then the order the nodes were given; both halves are contract, so two implementations answer byte-identically. Empty `nodes` is an ANSWER (no batches, width 0), not a refusal. Four refusals, in this order, one sentence each: `nodes[<i>].<field> must be ...` (an id that is not a string, depends_on not a list of strings, priority not an integer — named by position, never coerced), `duplicate node id <id>`, `node <id> depends on <dep>, which no node declares`, and `the graph has a cycle: <a> -> <b> -> <a>`. It reports what the graph PERMITS and decides nothing about what is safe to dispatch together: `depends_on` encodes logical order, not file contention.

nodes.title: Nodes

depends_on.description: Ids this node waits for; every one of them must be declared by some node. Optional: absent or null means none

priority.description: Tie-break inside a batch, descending. Optional; 0 when absent

nodes.description: The graph: one object per task, {id, depends_on?, priority?}. The order given is the tie-break inside a batch after priority.

tools.name: shiftwork_plan
tools.description: Shift-work plan: which units of a checkpoint may run NOW, and in what waves — the batches its `depends_on` graph permits, computed read-only from the file. Call it before dispatching a wave: `ready` (the first batch) is what shiftwork_clock_in will brief, and `width` is how many agents the widest wave needs. A `ready` member beyond the cursor is clockable only once clock-in has briefed it; without that brief, clock-out refuses it. Use shiftwork_status instead when you only want progress counts, and work_plan when the graph is yours to hand over as `nodes` rather than a checkpoint on disk — this tool reads the checkpoint's own plan.units. Units already `done` or `dropped` count as satisfied and are left out of every batch; `todo`, `in_progress` and `blocked` stay in. Order inside a batch is plan.units order, because the checkpoint schema has no priority field. It never moves plan.cursor — the cursor is echoed unchanged so the pointer and the batch view can be read side by side — and never writes anything. Refusals are structured, never exceptions: work_plan's sentences for a duplicate id, an unknown dependency or a cycle, and shiftwork_status's for a checkpoint it cannot read; a plan whose units are all terminal answers an empty `ready`, which is an answer, not a refusal. It reports logical order only: `depends_on` says nothing about two units writing the same file, so the orchestrator still decides what actually runs together.

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint
checkpoint.description: Path to the shift-work checkpoint JSON file (by convention .shiftwork/checkpoint.json in the repo the job works on), absolute or relative to the server's working directory. The same file shiftwork_plan, shiftwork_clock_in and shiftwork_clock_out take; it must validate against assets/schemas/shiftwork-checkpoint.json.

tools.name: memory_queries
tools.description: Write, or list the facts that still lack, the likely-prompt queries recall matches a user's prompt against — for each fact, the prompts a user would type when that fact is what they need. Call it with {} at the end of a session that saved facts, or when bantamkit_status reports `queries: n of m facts` with n below m: it answers up to 10 facts with no queries yet (layer, name, description, a body excerpt), the writing instructions, and `remaining`. Then call it with {"facts": [{name, layer?, queries}]} to store what you wrote. Every item is checked before anything is written and the first bad one refuses the whole call — an unknown name or layer, more than 8 queries, one over 200 characters; `queries: []` removes a fact's entry. No fact file changes: queries live in a per-layer sidecar under ~/.bantamkit/queries/, keyed to the fact's content, so a fact edited later is listed as missing again. memory_save takes `queries` directly for a fact you are saving now; this tool is for facts already on disk.

layer.description: project, profile, extra:<name> or native; optional: the first layer holding the name

queries.description: Up to 8 prompts, each at most 200 characters, in the user's language and in English; [] removes the fact's entry.

facts.description: Omit to list the facts missing queries

instructions:
# Memory

The runtime enforces format, dedupe, and budgets. You only decide WHEN and WHAT.

## Recall first

Before a task that resembles past work, call memory_recall with the words a
past-you would have used. Do this before acting, not after.

## When to save

- The user corrects you or states a preference → type "feedback"
- A durable fact about the user → "user", about ongoing work → "project",
  a URL/dashboard/ticket → "reference"
- Tag a lesson with outcome: error|success; close a project fact by saving it again with status: done.

## When NOT to save

- Anything derivable from the repo, git history, or docs
- One-off state that only matters in this conversation

## Writing the description

Write it to match the future recall QUERY, not to summarize the body.
Ask: "what words will future-me search with?" Put related memory names in links.
Fill keywords with the words the user will actually type, in their language — recall matches those too.

## Likely-prompt queries

When you save, also pass `queries`: three prompts in the user's language and three in English that a user would
type when this fact is what they need. Short and varied, technical terms kept in English, never more than five
words copied from the body. When `memory_queries` lists facts without queries, write theirs.

## On "duplicate" replies

If memory_save answers that a similar memory exists, either update it by
saving under that SAME name, or skip — never rename to force a second copy.

## Layers

Recall lines may start with `[project]`, `[extra:<name>]`, or `[profile]` —
where the fact came from. Prefer `[project]` when they conflict; saves always
go to the project store.
